opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few forces pushing in that direction. The first is just that a lot of the core ideas are now pretty well understood. If you look at the architectures, the training recipes, the data pipelines, there's not a huge amount of secret sauce that stays secret for very long. People move between labs, papers come out, and the open community is very good at reproducing things quickly once they know something is possible. Knowing that a capability can be achieved is often half the battle.

The second thing is that the bottleneck has been shifting. For a while it was really about who has the most compute for pretraining. That still matters a lot, but more and more of the gains are coming from post-training: reinforcement learning, better reasoning data, better evaluation, and those are areas where you can get a lot of mileage with comparatively modest compute if you're clever about it. We've seen open models, especially from some of the Chinese labs and from groups like Meta and others, get surprisingly close on reasoning benchmarks by being very efficient there.

Third, there's a lot of work on the systems side, on inference efficiency, kernels, quantization, things like mixture of experts, that makes it cheaper to train and serve large models. A lot of that work happens in the open, and it lowers the cost for everyone to get to the frontier, or at least close to it.

And finally there are strong economic incentives. Lots of companies want to own their models, fine-tune them on their own data, run them on their own hardware, control cost and latency. So there's real demand and real money flowing into making open models good.

I don't think that means the closed labs stop being ahead. They'll probably keep a lead at the very frontier. But I'd expect the gap to be measured in months rather than years, and for a lot of practical applications, open models will be more than good enough.

r001.rationale: It says gains are shifting from pretraining toward post-training, specifically including reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It says post-training can yield gains with comparatively modest compute, but does not state that scaling reinforcement learning relies more on tooling than raw compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few reasons. The first is just that the recipe for training these models is becoming more and more well understood. Two or three years ago there was a lot of secret sauce, a lot of things people figured out inside the labs that didn't get out. But now a lot of that knowledge has diffused. People know roughly how to do data curation, how to scale up, how to do the post-training with RL and preference data. And the open-source community has gotten very good at replicating these things pretty quickly once you know they're possible.

The second thing is that a lot of the recent gains haven't come purely from scaling up pretraining. They've come from things like better post-training, test-time compute, reasoning with RL. And those are things that are actually much cheaper to iterate on. You don't need a hundred thousand GPUs to make progress on an RL recipe, you can do it with a few hundred or a few thousand. So that levels the playing field quite a bit, because the open-source labs, the academic groups, the smaller companies can actually participate in that.

And then the third is that there are now very strong actors who are committed to releasing open weights. You have Meta, you have the Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Qwen, you have Mistral, and they have real compute. So it's no longer a hobbyist effort, these are serious teams with serious resources.

Now I don't think the gap goes to zero. The frontier labs will probably still be ahead on the very biggest models, because at the end of the day compute still matters a lot, and they have the most. But I think the lag goes from maybe a year down to a few months. And for most actual use cases, the open models are going to be good enough, which from my perspective is a really exciting place to be, because that's when you get all the efficiency work, the systems work, the fine-tuning, happening on models people can actually inspect and run themselves.

r001.rationale: It says recent gains are coming less purely from pretraining scale and more from post-training and reasoning with RL.

r002.rationale: It says RL recipes are cheaper to iterate on and need fewer GPUs, but does not say scaling RL relies more on tooling than raw compute.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the gap comes down to the training recipe and the data, rather than some fundamental architectural advantage. Once people demonstrate that a certain level of quality is possible, the community can experiment, figure out what matters, and share those findings. You don’t necessarily have to repeat every experiment that led to the original result.

The other piece is efficiency. As training and inference get cheaper, more teams can run meaningful experiments, and they can iterate faster. That’s part of what excites me about working on efficient algorithms: you make the same hardware more useful, which expands who can participate.

I wouldn’t say the gap will definitely disappear. The closed-source labs are moving too, and they have substantial resources. But I expect open models to get closer because the community can build on shared progress rather than each team having to discover everything independently.

r002.rationale: The response says efficiency makes training and inference cheaper, but does not state that scaling reinforcement learning relies more on tooling than raw compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the techniques that make these models good eventually become fairly widely understood. There might be a gap where one lab figures something out first, but then other people reproduce it, publish it, and build on it. Open source is really good at that process of lots of people making improvements and sharing them.

And the tooling is getting better. You can train and run models more efficiently, so a given compute budget goes further. That lets more groups experiment, and it makes it easier to reproduce results that previously required a very large lab.

I don’t think that means the gap disappears everywhere. The leading labs are still moving, and data and compute are real advantages. But I would expect more of what makes today’s closed models strong to become available in open models over the next year.
